newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE FLOURISH IN THE SPRINGTIME.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE FLOURISH IN THE SPRINGTIME.

text.p: France flourished in the Parisian springtime on Saturday by romping to their first grand slam on home soil in the final match at Parc des Princes.
Two tries in each half and another immaculate display of place kicking from centre Christophe Lamaison gave the French a comfortable 47-20 victory over Scotland.
In Cardiff, England confirmed their current supremacy among the four home nations by beating Wales 34-13 for their fifth Triple Crown in seven seasons.
It was also the final rugby union international to be staged at Cardiff Arms Park.
France, cruelly afflicted by injuries to key players throughout the season, were efficient when it mattered and expansive in the final 10 minutes once victory was confirmed.
They led 26-13 at halftime through tries to captain Abdel Benazzi and Laurent Leflamand, the latter resulting from a sweeping move sparked by full-back Jean-Luc Sadourny.
"It was catch-up rugby from the start," Scotland coach Richie Dixon conceded. "The players surrendered from the kick-off and there was very little they could do."
Prop Franck Tournaire put the issue beyond doubt with a try after the interval and, as the French crowd chorused La Marseillaise, their heroes turned on the style.
Throwing the ball around with abandon despite being pinned on their own line, the ball rippled through the backline for flanker Oliver Magne to touch down eight minutes from time.
Each of the French substitutes was given a run and the side lingered on the pitch long after the final whistle.
"It was such a great feeling, I just wanted to stay there," said Lamaison, who kicked 24 points in all.
From next year France, who clinched their four previous grand slams on foreign soil, will play at the new Stade de France under construction in the Paris suburb of St Denis.
England, despite playing most of the first half in Welsh territory, led by just three points at halftime.
They then cut loose in a 23-minute burst with four tries, two of them inspired by the guile of centre Jeremy Guscott, one of nine replacements to take the field.
The Arms Park, field of dreams for generations of Welsh schoolboys, will be flattened at the end of the season and redeveloped for the 1999 Rugby World Cup.
Fittingly the final points came from two players representing the future and past of Welsh rugby.
Scrum-half Rob Howley capped a wonderful game by weaving through some indifferent defence to score. Thirty-four-year old fly-half Jonathan Davies, playing his last match for Wales, converted.
